title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
explain_beginner: The paper studies how to make language models better at reasoning. Instead of letting a model produce one line of thought and answer, the authors let it produce several different lines of thought. They then pick the answer that appears most often across those attempts. The idea is that a hard problem can be solved in different ways, but the correct answer should usually be the same. Tests on arithmetic and common sense tasks showed clear gains, such as 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 11.0 percent on SVAMP. This matters because a simple change can make model answers more reliable without training a new model.
explain_business: This paper shows that a language model can answer complex reasoning questions more accurately if it is allowed to try several reasoning routes and then give the answer most of them support. The authors report large improvements on arithmetic and common sense tests, including 17.9 percent on GSM8K and 12.2 percent on AQuA. For executives, this suggests a practical reliability check: when an AI answer matters, ask for multiple attempts and use the consensus. The editor's note calls this a cheap control that an audit can recommend for high stakes answers. It informs decisions about how to review or deploy AI outputs in sensitive settings.
explain_practitioner: The authors introduce a decoding method for step by step prompting. Rather than taking only the single highest probability output, their approach generates many varied reasoning traces. It then chooses the answer that is most common after combining the evidence from those traces. This relies on the idea that different valid solution routes should converge on one correct answer. They tested the method on several arithmetic and common sense reasoning datasets. The reported gains over standard step by step prompting were 17.9 percent on GSM8K, 11.0 percent on SVAMP, 12.2 percent on AQuA, 6.4 percent on StrategyQA, and 3.9 percent on ARC challenge.
